analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate June 16, 2026 by Sen. Schumer with 6 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would quadruple the federal excise tax on corporate stock buybacks, from 1% to 4% of the value of the repurchased shares. A 1% buyback tax already exists in law; this bill raises it. It would also close an offset: under current law, companies can reduce their taxable buyback amount by the value of new stock they issue, and the bill would deny that offset for stock issued to highly paid executives and other employees earning over $1 million a year. The higher rate would apply to buybacks after the bill is enacted.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers in general, through added revenue to the Treasury from a 4% buyback tax instead of 1% [S2]. Anyone who thinks companies should direct cash toward investment, wages, or dividends rather than share repurchases also benefits to the extent the higher tax changes corporate behavior, though the bill contains no requirement that companies spend the money differently.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4% of the repurchase value under IRC section 4501(a), making buybacks meaningfully more expensive relative to dividends, debt paydown, investment, or wages.

Ends the practice (under section 4501(c)(3)) of letting companies shrink their taxable buyback base by the value of stock they issue to covered executives and to any person earning over $1 million in annual compensation, a pairing critics call funding executive pay while buying back stock.

Because it is an excise tax on every repurchase, the 4% rate raises federal revenue on each dollar of buybacks, with the money going to the general Treasury; the bill includes transition rules applying the new rate to repurchases after enactment and prorating offsets in the enactment-year taxable year.

analysis.who_pays: Large public corporations that repurchase their own stock, and their shareholders, pay the higher 4% excise tax on every dollar of buybacks. Since corporate stock is held disproportionately by the wealthiest households, the direct cost falls mainly on wealthy investors, though retirement savers holding index funds own some of those shares too. Executives and other employees earning over $1 million a year are the specific group whose stock-based compensation would no longer offset the company's buyback tax.

drawbacks.text: An excise tax on buybacks is ultimately borne by the company's shareholders, including ordinary retirement savers whose 401(k)s and index funds hold the same shares; the bill does not distinguish between buybacks that enrich executives and buybacks that simply return cash to all owners of the company.
A 4% tax is a modest drag, not a ban: it may raise revenue without changing corporate behavior much, since companies routinely repurchase stock when the price move on any given day is larger than 4%.

The new exception to the offset rule adds compliance complexity, requiring companies to track which issued shares went to covered employees and to anyone earning over $1 million, and it applies to taxable years ending more than 90 days after enactment on a prospective basis that companies must plan around.
The bill has no Republican cosponsors, so even if enacted it could be repealed by a later Congress, and the revenue it raises is not earmarked for any specific public purpose in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a real but incremental change, not a structural reform. Quadrupling the buyback tax and closing the executive-stock offset raises revenue from a small, identifiable group — big repurchasing corporations and their (mostly wealthy) shareholders — and modestly tilts the playing field away from buybacks. But 4% is unlikely to stop buybacks on its own, the revenue is unearmarked, and shareholders broadly, including retirement savers, absorb some of the cost. The bill is well targeted and inexpensive to comply with relative to its purpose, but its public benefit depends on revenue use and corporate behavior the bill itself does not control.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day of introduction, June 16, 2026, with no markup, hearing, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the Stock Buyback Accountability Act of 2026 in the Senate on June 16, 2026, joined by Sens. Wyden, Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, and Whitehouse as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the recorded action history contains no further activity.
All 7 supporters listed are Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored the bill.

key_actors.name: Sen. Charles E. Schumer
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 16, 2026, raising the buyback excise tax from 1% to 4% and narrowing the offset for stock issued to highly paid employees.

key_actors.name: Sens. Wyden, Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, and Whitehouse
key_actors.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's six original cosponsors on introduction, giving it 7 Senate supporters, all Democrats.

key_actors.name: Senate Committee on Finance
key_actors.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 16, 2026; the action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote scheduled since.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been pending in the Senate Finance Committee since June 16, 2026, with the 119th Congress ending January 3, 2027. Bills referred to Finance with no committee action within a few months of session's end and no cosponsors from the other party rarely receive a markup, let alone a floor vote. Unless the committee schedules action in the remaining months, the bill will die at the end of the Congress and would need to be reintroduced in the 120th.
